scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: What if the decorator needs a setting, such as how many times to repeat? We add one more level.

scenes.onScreen: "Three levels": three numbered lines (1. Outer function takes the decorator's settings; 2. Middle function takes the function to wrap; 3. Inner function is the wrapper that runs) and an analogy card: a wrapping machine with a dial: first you set the dial, then it takes a gift, then it wraps
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A decorator with arguments is a function that returns a decorator. So there are three levels. The outer function takes the settings, such as times. It returns the middle function, which is the real decorator, and takes the function to wrap. That returns the inner wrapper, which runs each time. When you write at repeat of three, Python first calls repeat with three, gets the decorator, and applies it. Think of a wrapping machine with a dial. First you set the dial. Then you hand over the gift.

Python calls repeat with three first, and then applies the result to hello. [HL 10] The function. [HL 11] It prints hello and a name. [HL 13] One call, and we see Hello Asha three times.

Three: The decorator takes the function and returns the wrapper. Four: at repeat of 3 first calls repeat of 3, then applies the result. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: one level of nesting is missing
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Repeat returns the wrapper directly. But at repeat of three means, call repeat, then call the result with hello. So the wrapper runs immediately, with hello as an argument, and looks for func. Name error, name func is not defined. Add the middle level, a decorator function that takes func.

props.error:
File "repeat.py", line 4, in wrapper
    func(*args, **kwargs)
    ^^^^
NameError: name 'func' is not defined
props.why: At repeat of three calls repeat, and then calls the result with the function. If repeat returns the wrapper directly, the wrapper runs at once, and has no func to call.

pun: "Why did the decorator need three levels? It was a big fan of nesting."
challenge: Write a decorator shout(n) that prints the function's result in capital letters n times.
challengeAnswer: def shout(n): def decorator(func): def wrapper(*a, **k): for _ in range(n): print(func(*a, **k).upper()); return wrapper; return decorator.

shorts.title: Why three levels
shorts.hook: "A decorator with arguments has three levels."
shorts.script: A decorator with arguments has three levels. The outer function takes the setting. It returns the decorator. The decorator takes the function, and returns the wrapper. Setting first, function second, wrapper last. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Three levels, in order.

shorts.title: What the at line does
shorts.hook: "When you write at repeat of three, Python first calls repeat with three."
shorts.script: When you write at repeat of three, Python first calls repeat with three. That returns a decorator. Then Python calls that decorator with your function. So the brackets in the at line tell you there is an extra level. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Brackets mean an extra level.

shorts.title: Keep the name
shorts.script: Do not forget functools dot wraps. Put it above the inner wrapper, even in a decorator with arguments. Then the decorated function keeps its name and its doc string. Tools and error messages then show the right name. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Always use wraps.

shorts.title: Missing level
shorts.script: A bug that confuses everyone. Repeat returns the wrapper directly. At repeat of three then calls the wrapper with hello, and Python says, name error, name func is not defined. Add the middle level that takes func. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Add the middle level.
